title: Heartbreak
text:
Oh, I am tired! I have laughed so much,

so much that tears have risen to my eyes;

so much that this grimace twisting my mouth

is the strange trace of my crazed laughter.


So much that this intense pallor I wear

(as in portraits of an ancient lineage)

comes from the weariness of mad laughter

sliding its stupor through my entire body.


Oh, I am tired! Let me sleep;

for joy, like anguish, can make us ill.

What a strange idea—to say that I am sad!

When have you ever seen me happier than now?


A lie! I have no doubts, no jealousy,

no unrest, anguish, sorrow, or desire.

If moisture from tears shines in my eyes,

it is only from the effort of laughing so much…
editorial_note: The translation lets the speaker's denial expose itself through repetition, bodily fatigue, and forced brightness.

title: Like Spring
text:
Like a black wing I spread my hair

across your knees.

Closing your eyes, you breathed its fragrance,

then asked me:

“Do you sleep on moss-covered stones?

Do you bind your braids with willow branches?

Is clover your pillow? Is your hair so black

because you pressed into it the dark,

thick juice of wild blackberries?

What a fresh, strange fragrance surrounds you!

You smell of streams, of earth and forests.

What perfume do you wear?” Laughing, I told you:

“None, none!

I love you and I am young; I smell of spring.

The scent you breathe is firm flesh,

clear cheeks, and new blood.

I love you and I am young; that is why I carry

the very fragrances of spring!”
editorial_note: The erotic catalog remains rooted in landscape, youth, and an unperfumed body.

title: The Hour
text:
Take me now, while it is still early

and I carry fresh dahlias in my hand.


Take me now, while still dark

is this taciturn hair of mine.


Now, while my flesh is fragrant,

my eyes clear and my skin rose-pink.


Now, while my light foot wears

the living sandal of spring.


Now, while laughter rings on my lips

like a bell shaken in haste.


Later… oh, I know

that none of this will be mine then!


Then your desire will be useless,

like an offering laid upon a mausoleum.


Take me now, while it is still early

and my hand is rich with tuberoses!


Today, not later. Before night falls

and the fresh corolla withers.


Today, not tomorrow. Oh lover, can you not see

that the climbing vine will become a cypress?
editorial_note: The repeated now preserves the poem's carpe diem urgency; the final vine-to-cypress turn keeps its funerary shock.

title: The Fig Tree
text:
Because it is rough and ugly,

because all its branches are gray,

I feel pity for the fig tree.


In my orchard stand a hundred lovely trees:

round plum trees,

straight lemon trees,

and orange trees with glossy shoots.


In springtime

they all cover themselves in flowers

around the fig tree.


And the poor thing looks so sad,

with twisted boughs that never dress

in tightly gathered buds…


That is why,

each time I pass beside it,

I say, taking care

to make my voice sweet and cheerful:

“The fig tree is the loveliest

of all the trees in the orchard.”


If it hears me,

if it understands the language I speak,

what profound sweetness will make its nest

inside its sensitive tree-soul!


And perhaps at night,

when the wind fans its crown,

drunk with joy, it will tell it:

“Today someone called me beautiful.”
editorial_note: The fable-like tenderness remains plainspoken, allowing the final reported sentence its full emotional weight.

title: Rainy Night
text:
It is raining…

Wait, do not sleep;

listen closely to what the wind is saying

and what the water says as it taps

with tiny fingers on the panes.

How joyful the waving wheat must be!

How eagerly the grass will swell!

How many diamonds must now be hanging

from the deep branches of the pines!

Wait, do not sleep. Let us listen

to the rhythm of the rain.

Rest your brooding brow

between my breasts.

I shall feel the beat of your two temples,

pulsing and warm,

like two living hammers

striking my flesh.

Wait, do not sleep. Tonight

the two of us are one world,

set apart by wind and rain

inside the warm basin of a bedroom.

Wait, do not sleep. Tonight

perhaps we are the supreme root

from which tomorrow must arise

the beautiful trunk of a new people.
editorial_note: The rain's fertility and the lovers' enclosed world are preserved; raza becomes people to carry futurity without biological distortion.

title: Grappling Life
text:
Lover, if I die, do not take me to the cemetery.

Open my grave just beneath the earth, beside

the laughing, holy clamor of an aviary,

or by the enchanted conversation of a fountain.


Just beneath the earth, lover. Almost upon it,

where the sun may warm my bones, and my eyes,

lengthened into stems, may rise to see again

the wild lamp of red sunsets.


Just beneath the earth, lover, so the passage

may be shorter. I foresee

my flesh struggling to return upward,

to feel in every atom the freshness of the wind.


I know that perhaps my hands down there

will never remain still,

but always, like moles, will claw the soil

amid the crushed and thickened shadows.


Scatter seeds over me. I want them to root

in the yellow clay of my dwindled bones.

Up the earthen ladder of living roots

I shall climb to look at you through purple lilies!
editorial_note: The title interprets garfio as the body's grappling return; repeated proximity to earth sustains the poem's fierce material resurrection.

title: Sweet Miracle
text:
What is this? A wonder! My hands are flowering.

Roses, roses, roses grow from my fingers.

My lover kissed my hands, and from them—

oh grace!—roses sprang like stars.


I walk the road crying out the enchantment,

smiling and weeping by turns from happiness,

and beneath the miracle of my spell

the wings of the wind grow fragrant with roses.


People passing murmur when they see me:

“Can you not see she is mad? Take her home.

She says roses have grown from her hands

and waves them about like butterflies!”


Oh, poor people who never understand

a miracle such as this, who understand only

that roses grow solely on rosebushes,

and wheat nowhere but in fields of wheat!


Who demand line and color and form,

accepting only reality as law.

When someone says, “I walk with sweetness,”

they immediately look for the creature.


Let them call me mad, let them lock me in a cell,

let them close the door with seven keys,

let them place beside it a hound,

a harsh jailer, a faithful jailer.


Still I shall sing: “My hands are flowering.

Roses, roses, roses grow from my fingers.”

And my whole cell will carry the fragrance

of an immense bouquet of roses from France.
editorial_note: The ecstatic literalism is preserved against the onlookers' narrow realism; the repeated flowering remains incantatory.
